label: bidriware/chemistry/colours-of-the-alloy
title: The colours of bidri
description: Swatches of the bidri alloy before and after the fort-earth bath, and of its silver inlay, which keeps its colour. Place it beside the blackening step.

u0002.text: The fort-earth bath turns the alloy black and leaves the silver bright.

u0003.text: Sanding leaves the alloy zinc-white, and the boiling solution of fort earth and ammonium chloride blackens it.

u0008.text: The zinc alloy turns black while the silver keeps its colour.

u0013.text: The black ground contrasts with the lustrous silver inlay.

C004.text: The black background of bidri ware contrasts strikingly with its lustrous silver inlay.

quotes.quote: The contrast between the black oxidized background and lustrous silver inlay gives a beauty to the Bidri ware.
The inlays contrast strikingly with the matt black patina of the vessel.

C070.text: In tarkashi and tainishan work the inlaid surface is then filed or sanded level, and the temporary black vanishes to leave a smooth, zinc-white surface.

quotes.quote: filing the above piece with a flat iron file so that the embedded silver and the base material's surface form a smooth single level
This is done only in the case of tarkashi and taihnishan techniques.
the whole surface is again rubbed with sand paper or buffrng machine. Thereafter the temporary black colour vanishes and the surface becomes smooth and zinc-white.

C071.text: The finished article is dipped in a boiling solution of fort earth and ammonium chloride, which turns the zinc alloy black while the silver keeps its colour.

quotes.quote: The polished article is then dipped in a boiled solution of ammonium chloride and earth collected and available only from the fort area
By this process, the zinc portion ofthe articles become black and the silver portion retains its own colour.
The finished article is now given a dip in this hot solution.
The zinc alloy turns permanently jet black while the silver retains its brilliance.
